pronunciation.approximation: Say "ekkeko" — two open syllables with a light glottal catch between the double k in the Aymara-influenced pronunciation; stress falls on the penult.

kin.label: Aymara (traditional derivation)
kin.form: Often derived from Aymara ikiqu/iqiqu, 'dwarf' — the traditional explanation of the lexicon gloss 'The dwarf', not philologically proven.

kin.label: Spanish spellings
kin.form: Ekeko, Equeco — the hispanicized forms used by colonial chroniclers and in the modern fair tradition.

kin.label: Consort
kin.form: Coya — his beloved in the founding legend recorded by Antonio Díaz Villamil (1904).

pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "ekkeko" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Ekkeko" preserves the name's scholarly dignity. The name's own etymology is uncertain: the gloss 'dwarf' rests on a proposed Aymara derivation (ikiqu) that handbooks record as plausible rather than proven. The entry is Tier 2: the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops.

domains.title: Ekkeko
domains.subtitle: Luck
domains.lead: Ekkeko is the Andean god of luck and abundance: a smiling little man bowed under a pack holding everything a household could wish for. His mythology is young as myths go — a colonial chronicler's notice, a founding legend printed in 1904, and a January fair where all of La Paz buys its dreams in miniature — but it rests on burden-carrier figurines far older than the name.

cards.name: God of Plenty
cards.desc: The loaded pack on his back carries every good thing a household can hope for: grain, coin, houses, health, and a lit pipe besides.

cards.name: The Alasitas Fair
cards.desc: Every 24 January the streets of La Paz fill with miniatures of everything people want, bought, blessed, and set on his altar to be grown into reality.

cards.name: Household Idol
cards.desc: Bernabé Cobo described how Andean families kept his little image by the hearth, loading it with tiny packs and offerings so prosperity would stay in the house.

cards.name: Consort of Coya
cards.desc: In the legend recorded in 1904, Ekeko fed his beloved Coya from his own flesh during a famine; her faithful search restored him as the little clay god.

symbols.name: The loaded pack
symbols.meaning: The bundle of goods on his back — every modest desire of the household, abundance compressed into one bowed, patient burden.

symbols.name: Clay figurine
symbols.meaning: Pre-Columbian Tiwanaku figures of burden-carriers are the archaeological ancestors of the modern Ekeko images.

symbols.name: Miniatures (alasitas)
symbols.meaning: The tiny objects of the fair — money, houses, cars, diplomas — wishes bought small so the god can grow them large.

symbols.name: The ritual offering cloth
symbols.meaning: The mesa laden with sugar figurines, seeds, and breads set before the idol on his feast day.

symbols.name: The pipe
symbols.meaning: The little clay pipe of folk images, an emblem of contentment and the unhurried ease of a well-fed house.

mythology.lead: Ekeko's mythology is unusual: nearly all of it is modern. A colonial Jesuit notices the household idol in 1653; a founding legend is printed in 1904; the January fair of Alasitas keeps the cult alive in the streets of La Paz. Beneath all of it lie burden-carrier figurines from Tiwanaku, a thousand years older than the name.

myths.title: Ekeko and Coya in the Famine
myths.text: The best-known story of Ekeko is surprisingly recent: it was printed in 1904 by the Bolivian writer Antonio Díaz Villamil in his Exaltación de la Alasita. In the time of drought, when the storehouses stood empty, the little man Ekeko fed his beloved Coya from his own flesh, cutting pieces from his body so that she would not starve. When the rains finally returned, Coya searched the hills for him and found only a small clay figure bowed under an enormous load. She recognized her lover in the idol, carried it home, and set it on the household altar; from that day, abundance never left her house. Scholars treat the legend as modern folklore rather than pre-Columbian scripture — and say so openly — yet it explains everything the ritual actually does: the little body, the heavy pack, the beloved who keeps him. The myth reads Ekeko as love converted into provision.

myths.title: The Little God Cobo Saw
myths.text: Bernabé Cobo, writing his Historia del Nuevo Mundo in 1653, is the earliest secure witness. Among the household devotions of the Andean people he describes a small idol called Equeco, revered as a god of wealth and contentment: his image was a little figure loaded with packs and bundles, set up in the house and offered food, so that he would keep the family supplied with the small goods of life — food, clothing, coin. Cobo's Equeco is no state god of the Sun's rank but a humble domestic numen, carried and coddled by ordinary households. That a Jesuit chronicler should pause over so modest a deity is itself testimony to how thoroughly the little god had entered daily life. The passage anchors Ekeko in the colonial record and shows what he was always for: not empire or war, but the prosperity of the kitchen and the storeroom.

myths.title: Alasitas, the Buying of Dreams
myths.text: Every January the city of La Paz holds the Alasitas fair, and the streets fill with miniature versions of everything people want: tiny houses, banknotes, cars, diplomas, sewing machines, even tiny marriage certificates. The name is Aymara — 'buy for me' — and the transaction is a prayer: you purchase the miniature, carry it to be blessed — by priest and by the ritual ch'alla of sprinkled alcohol alike — and set it on the household altar before your Ekeko, who is charged with growing the little thing into the real one during the coming year. The fair's patron is Ekeko himself; his image, pipe in mouth and pack on back, presides over the commerce. The rite was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the 2010s. Its engine is sympathetic magic, but its meaning is bolder: it treats desire as a legitimate offering and commerce as a form of hope.

myths.title: The Burden-Carriers of Tiwanaku
myths.text: Long before any text named him, the high plateau produced his image. Among the burial goods of Tiwanaku (c. 500–1000 CE), archaeologists recover small ceramic figurines of men bent under packs, head-straps cutting across their foreheads — exactly the posture of the modern Ekeko. Whether these burden-carriers were 'Ekeko' in any sense we can recover is honestly unknown: the Tiwanaku left no deciphered writings, and the identification is the work of modern scholarship and artisan tradition rather than proof. But the continuity is visual and, in a way, theological — a culture imagined prosperity as something carried on a humble human back. The museums of La Paz display the ancient figurines beside the modern ones. The myth's deepest layer says that luck is not lightning but load-bearing: abundance arrives as something small, bowed, and patient.

lore.syncretism: Ekeko is a study in colonial layering. His name and image passed into Spanish as Ekeko or Equeco; his consort bears Coya, the title of the Inca empress; and his fair was folded into Catholic time — the January date in La Paz is bound up with the feast of Our Lady of Peace, and priests bless the miniature purchases even as the Church has periodically denounced the whole commerce as idolatry. The blessing is the syncretism in one gesture: sacrament and ch'alla sprinkling the same little car. Under the colonial surface the substrate is older — Aymara marketplace piety and the burden-carrier imagery of Tiwanaku — so that the 'little god' condenses three strata: pre-Columbian figurine, colonial household saint, and republican national emblem.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ekeko is today a national emblem of Bolivia, printed on lottery tickets, staged in civic pageants, and set on altars in houses that no longer remember the famine legend. The Alasitas fair has travelled with Bolivian migration — to Buenos Aires, Santiago, and the Peruvian highlands, where Puno keeps its own January fair — so the little god now presides over diaspora longing as much as over household luck. Twentieth-century letters and art reworked the Díaz Villamil legend into schoolbooks, murals, and popular song. UNESCO recognition fixed the fair on the world stage. Through it all the image barely changes: a small smiling man under a heavy pack, the patron of everyone who wants ordinary things — a roof, a wage, a full table — and asks for them the Andean way, in miniature first.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ekeko is the god of wanting precisely. Where state religions promise salvation and warrior cults promise glory, he promises the small, exact things of a life: a house, a harvest, a child's health, a little smoke from a clay pipe. His liturgy is shopping — but shopping understood as the materialization of hope. To buy the miniature house is to admit you want the house, to say so publicly, and to give the wanting a place to wait. There is a quiet theology in that: desire is not vain if it is offered; it becomes vain only when it is hidden. The bowed back of the figurine completes the lesson. Abundance, in the Andes, is not lightning from heaven but something carried — patiently, humbly, load by load — until the pack becomes the house.
